body:
Morgan Stanley is restricting withdrawals from its flagship private credit vehicle for a third straight quarter, underscoring how the $1.8 trillion market continues to work through a stubborn backlog of redemption requests even as overall pressure shows signs of easing.

The North Haven Private Income Fund, which oversees roughly $7 billion in assets, capped repurchases at 5% of shares for the third quarter after investors asked to pull out 11.4%, according to a shareholder letter dated Sept. 18. The request level was nearly unchanged from the prior quarter's 11.6%.

Completed repurchases across the three periods through September will total approximately $479 million, the fund said. Nearly two-thirds of the latest withdrawal requests came from investors whose earlier attempts had already been limited during the previous two repurchase offers.

"We believe the composition and stabilization of request activity may indicate the durability of the company's investor base," the fund said in an investor update. "Upon completion of this quarter's repurchases, investors who sought full tender of their units during the prior two repurchase offers will have received more than 80% of their requested tendered amount."

The hit to the fund's net asset value is expected to be roughly $101 million after accounting for new subscriptions and dividend reinvestments.

The restrictions place Morgan Stanley alongside peers including Blackstone and BlackRock, which have also continued to limit investor exits from private credit vehicles. Fund managers across the industry are still contending with roughly $15 billion in unfulfilled withdrawal requests following a record rush for the exits over the past year.

Investor concerns have centered on underwriting standards in the private credit space and lenders' exposure to older software investments, a key borrower base for direct lenders that faces potential disruption from artificial intelligence.

The structure of these non-traded funds typically allows periodic redemption windows but with built-in caps designed to prevent forced asset sales when demand spikes. When requests exceed the limit, investors may receive only a portion of what they asked for, leaving them to reapply in subsequent quarters.

A separate Morgan Stanley vehicle, North Haven Private Income Fund A, with less than $1 billion in total investments, also restricted redemptions after receiving requests covering about 6.8% of its shares, down slightly from 7.2% in the prior quarter. It will likewise repurchase 5% of shares.

While redemption requests at major funds have largely declined in the most recent quarter, they remain elevated by historical standards. Wealthy individual investors have pulled money from private credit products in recent months amid concerns about lending quality and the durability of software-focused loan portfolios.

Data from large private credit vehicles managed by Apollo, Ares, and Blue Owl is expected to be released in the coming weeks, offering further insight into whether the easing trend holds across the broader market.

Morgan Stanley's largest shareholder is Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, which reported a 23.95% beneficial stake, or 380,307,520 shares, as of March 31, according to its latest Schedule 13D filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission. The standstill and preemptive rights in MUFG's investor agreement with the bank now run to October 2028.

MUFG is also entering the very asset class at the center of this story. On Sept. 1, it announced separate talks with BlackRock and Morgan Stanley Investment Management to build an open platform for institutional investment in Japanese private credit. BlackRock manages the HPS Corporate Lending Fund listed above, and its private financing platform, built on the 2025 acquisition of HPS Investment Partners, oversees about $388 billion in client assets. Morgan Stanley Investment Management has provided debt solutions to companies worldwide for more than 15 years. People familiar with the plans said the collaborations aim to originate ¥200 billion to ¥300 billion of subordinated debt over the next few years.

Japan's private credit market remains small next to those in the US and Europe, and MUFG has made the segment a priority even as the US market it is drawing on works through its largest redemption backlog on record. The president of MUFG Bank said in April that the group did not expect to book a sizeable loss from private credit.
